summary.text: The ninth term is \((2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19\cdot23)^2+1=49{,}770{,}428{,}644{,}836{,}901=29^2\cdot59{,}180{,}057{,}841{,}661\). Thus it is not squarefree, so the conjunction is false regardless of the claim about infinitely many prime terms.

full_proof.text:
Let \(p_0=2,p_1=3,p_2=5,\ldots\) denote the primes in increasing order, with indexing beginning at \(0\), and define
\[
P_n=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}p_k,
\qquad
a(n)=P_n^2+1.
\]
Thus \(P_n\) is the product of the first \(n\) primes. We will show that \(a(9)\) is not squarefree.

The first nine primes are
\[
2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23.
\]
This list can be checked elementarily: each listed number has no prime divisor at most its square root, while every integer between \(2\) and \(23\) not on the list is composite. Hence, in the indexing above, \(p_0=2,\ldots,p_8=23\), and therefore
\[
P_9=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19\cdot23.
\]
Successive multiplication gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
2\cdot3&=6,\\
6\cdot5&=30,\\
30\cdot7&=210,\\
210\cdot11&=2310,\\
2310\cdot13&=30030,\\
30030\cdot17&=510510,\\
510510\cdot19&=9699690,\\
9699690\cdot23&=223092870.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
P_9=223092870
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(9)
 &=223092870^2+1\\
 &=49770428644836900+1\\
 &=49770428644836901.
\end{aligned}
\]

Now \(29\) is prime: a composite number of size \(29\) would have a prime divisor no larger than \(\sqrt{29}<6\), so it would be divisible by one of \(2,3,5\); direct inspection shows that \(29\) is divisible by none of these. Moreover, the following exact multiplication holds:
\[
29^2\cdot59180057841661
=841\cdot59180057841661
=49770428644836901.
\]
Combining this with the value of \(a(9)\), we obtain
\[
29^2\mid a(9).
\]

A positive integer is squarefree only if the square of no prime divides it (equivalently, every prime in its prime factorization occurs with exponent at most one). Since the square of the prime \(29\) divides \(a(9)\), the number \(a(9)\) is not squarefree.

Thus the assertion
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb N,\quad a(n)\text{ is squarefree}
\]
is false, with \(n=9\) as an explicit counterexample. The stated conjecture is the conjunction of this universal squarefreeness assertion and the assertion that \(a(n)\) is prime for infinitely many \(n\). A conjunction is false as soon as either conjunct is false, so the counterexample at \(n=9\) disproves the stated combined conjecture. This argument does not need to decide, and makes no claim about, the separate question of whether infinitely many terms of the sequence are prime.
